contradictions.question: How many of Bani's offspring returned from Babylon?
contradictions.summary: Ezra 2:10 says the children of Bani who returned from Babylon numbered 642. Nehemiah 7:15, which is supposed to be the same census of the same returnees, gives 648 and even names the family head differently (Binnui rather than Bani). Same event, different totals, different patriarch.
contradictions.commentary:
Ezra 2 and Nehemiah 7 are not two independent rosters. They are two versions of the same document — the registry of the first wave of exiles who came back under Sheshbazzar/Zerubbabel. The text of Nehemiah 7:5 explicitly says Nehemiah found 'the book of the genealogy of those who came up at the first' and copied it into his own record. So this is one list, transmitted twice, and the numbers do not match.

The apologist playbook here is well-rehearsed. Gleason Archer's Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties suggests one list counts those who originally signed up and the other counts those who actually showed up, with deaths and defections accounting for the gaps. Others propose scribal copying errors in the numerals, which is a much more honest move. The 'two-census' theory does not survive contact with the text — Nehemiah is not running a second census, he is explicitly reproducing an earlier register. And the Binnui/Bani swap is a giveaway: this is one family name transmitted through two textual streams, with one stream preferring one spelling and the other stream preferring the other. That is exactly what we would expect from manuscript drift, not from a deliberate update.

Critical scholarship on Ezra-Nehemiah, from Williamson to Blenkinsopp to Klein, treats these numerical divergences as evidence of textual corruption in transmission, not theological signal. Hebrew numerals were written out as words in this period, but the underlying figures are unstable across the Masoretic Text, the Septuagint, and 1 Esdras — and 1 Esdras 5 gives yet a third set of numbers for several of these families (and aligns with one or the other of the Hebrew witnesses for the rest). When you have multiple witnesses and divergent totals, the most parsimonious conclusion is that scribes miscopied, not that God inspired contradictory accounting.

For the inerrantist this is a real problem, because both Ezra 2 and Nehemiah 7 claim to be reproducing the same source document. You cannot rescue the numbers by appealing to different perspectives or different time periods — the text itself rules that out. Either the original document had one number and one of the two transmissions corrupted it, or both transmissions have drifted from an original we no longer possess. Either way, the doctrine of a perfectly preserved text takes a hit. Take your pick.
scholarship: H. G. M. Williamson, Ezra, Nehemiah, Word Biblical Commentary 16 (Word Books, 1985), pp. 28-32.
Joseph Blenkinsopp, Ezra-Nehemiah: A Commentary, Old Testament Library (Westminster John Knox, 1988), pp. 83-87.
Ralph W. Klein, 'Ezra-Nehemiah, Books of,' in The Anchor Bible Dictionary, Vol. 2, ed. David Noel Freedman (Doubleday, 1992), pp. 731-742.
Lester L. Grabbe, A History of the Jews and Judaism in the Second Temple Period, Vol. 1: Yehud (T&T Clark, 2004), pp. 285-291.
Gleason L. Archer, Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties (Zondervan, 1982), pp. 229-232.
Jacob M. Myers, Ezra, Nehemiah, Anchor Bible 14 (Doubleday, 1965), pp. 14-18.

The children of Binnui, six hundred forty and eight. Nehemiah 7:15

contradictions.question: How many of Bebai's offspring returned from Babylon?
contradictions.summary: Ezra 2:11 reports 623 children of Bebai returned from Babylon. Nehemiah 7:16 gives 628 for the same family in the same returnee list. Five-person discrepancy in a roster that both texts claim to be reproducing from the same source document.
contradictions.commentary:
This is another data point in the Ezra 2 versus Nehemiah 7 divergence problem, and it deserves to be treated as part of the same pattern rather than as a standalone puzzle. The two lists are not independent — Nehemiah 7:5 is explicit that the chapter is a copy of the original returnee registry. Yet across roughly two dozen family entries, the numbers disagree more than half the time. That is a transmission problem.

The standard harmonization, which goes back at least to Keil-Delitzsch in the nineteenth century, is that one list was taken at a different point in time than the other — people died, people changed their minds, people had children. That sounds tidy until you actually run the math. The Ezra and Nehemiah totals do not just drift in one direction; some families gain people and other families lose people. If this were genuine attrition or growth, you would expect some directional pattern. You don't get one. You get the random walk you would expect from scribes miscopying numerals.

Williamson in his WBC volume and Blenkinsopp in his OTL volume both point to the fact that 1 Esdras 5 — a Greek text reproducing essentially the same list — sometimes agrees with Ezra against Nehemiah, sometimes with Nehemiah against Ezra, and sometimes gives a third number entirely. For Bebai specifically, 1 Esdras 5:13 reads 623 (agreeing with Ezra against Nehemiah's 628), which makes Nehemiah the likely site of the corruption. That kind of two-against-one alignment is exactly how textual critics triangulate the original reading. Hebrew scribes were generally careful, but numerical material is notoriously the first thing to drift, because numbers carry no semantic redundancy — there is nothing in the sentence around the number to help a scribe catch a slip.

The apologist needs both numbers to be correct, because both books claim divine origin and both claim to be reproducing the same source. The critical scholar just needs the texts to be human documents that drifted in transmission, which is exactly what the manuscript evidence shows. One of those positions has a mechanism. The other has a problem.
scholarship: H. G. M. Williamson, Ezra, Nehemiah, Word Biblical Commentary 16 (Word Books, 1985), pp. 28-32.
Joseph Blenkinsopp, Ezra-Nehemiah: A Commentary, Old Testament Library (Westminster John Knox, 1988), pp. 83-87.
Sara Japhet, From the Rivers of Babylon to the Highlands of Judah: Collected Studies on the Restoration Period (Eisenbrauns, 2006), pp. 366-372.
C. F. Keil and F. Delitzsch, Commentary on the Old Testament, Vol. 4: Ezra, Nehemiah, Esther (T&T Clark, 1873), pp. 36-40.
Jacob M. Myers, Ezra, Nehemiah, Anchor Bible 14 (Doubleday, 1965), pp. 14-18.

answers.answerExplanation: The children of Bebai, six hundred twenty and three. Ezra 2:11
The children of Bebai, six hundred twenty and eight. Nehemiah 7:16

contradictions.question: How many of Azgad's offspring returned from Babylon?
contradictions.summary: Ezra 2:12 counts 1,222 returnees from the family of Azgad. Nehemiah 7:17 gives 2,322 for the same family in the same roster. This is not a five-person rounding error — the two numbers differ by 1,100 people.
contradictions.commentary:
This is one of the more spectacular numerical disagreements in the Ezra/Nehemiah parallel and it is exactly the kind of case where the apologist's 'maybe people died between censuses' explanation completely falls apart. The discrepancy is 1,100 people in a single family. You do not lose or gain a thousand people from one family entry through normal demographic drift between two near-contemporary records of the same event.

What you do get is a perfectly recognizable scribal mechanism. In Hebrew, the numbers 'one thousand' (eleph) and 'two thousand' (alpayim) are visually close, and the units and hundreds positions can be confused in early square-script manuscripts. 1 Esdras 5:13 — an independent Greek transmission of the same list — gives 1,322 in the main text (close to Ezra's 1,222) with variant readings of 3,222 and 3,622 in some witnesses, showing that the textual tradition was unstable across multiple streams. This is not a 'God said it twice with a different emphasis' situation. This is a numerical roster that scribes could not keep stable.

Williamson in WBC 16 notes that the Azgad numbers in particular are 'almost certainly corrupt' in at least one of the two Hebrew witnesses, and Blenkinsopp concurs. Critical scholarship has largely stopped trying to defend the integrity of these numbers and treats them as a textbook case of why we cannot speak of a single, stable, perfectly preserved Hebrew text. The numbers in Kings versus Chronicles, the genealogies of Genesis 5 and 11 across MT/LXX/SP, and these Ezra/Nehemiah totals all show the same pattern: numerical data is exactly where transmission fails.

The apologetic move of choice — 'one is a count from before the journey, the other after' — does not work for a discrepancy this large. You would need a thousand-person catastrophe localized to a single family while every other family stays stable or grows. There is no such mechanism in the text. The honest read is that we have a corrupted number somewhere in the transmission, and inerrancy as classically formulated does not survive that admission.
scholarship: H. G. M. Williamson, Ezra, Nehemiah, Word Biblical Commentary 16 (Word Books, 1985), pp. 28-32.
Joseph Blenkinsopp, Ezra-Nehemiah: A Commentary, Old Testament Library (Westminster John Knox, 1988), pp. 83-87.
Loring W. Batten, A Critical and Exegetical Commentary on the Books of Ezra and Nehemiah, International Critical Commentary (T&T Clark, 1913), pp. 80-85.
Zipora Talshir, I Esdras: From Origin to Translation, SBL Septuagint and Cognate Studies 47 (Society of Biblical Literature, 1999), pp. 246-251.
Emanuel Tov, Textual Criticism of the Hebrew Bible, 3rd ed. (Fortress, 2012), pp. 11-13.

contradictions.question: How many of Adonikam's offspring returned from Babylon?
contradictions.summary: Ezra 2:13 has 666 sons of Adonikam returning from Babylon. Nehemiah 7:18, copying the same registry, gives 667. A single-digit discrepancy in a number that the biblical text says is precise to the individual.
contradictions.commentary:
On a percentage basis this is the smallest of the Ezra/Nehemiah discrepancies in the family rolls, and the apologist will of course point to that — one person, what's the big deal. The point is not the size of the gap. The point is that there is a gap at all in a list that both books claim to be transmitting from a common source document. Nehemiah 7:5 explicitly frames the chapter as a reproduction of 'the book of the genealogy of those who came up at the first.' One source, two copies, two different numbers.

The traditional harmonization here is that someone died on the road or someone joined late, and the two figures reflect two different snapshots in time. Keil-Delitzsch leaned on this in the nineteenth century and Archer continues it in his Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties. The problem with the time-snapshot defense is that it has to be deployed dozens of times across the chapter, with the numbers drifting in both directions, and it never explains why Nehemiah — who is reproducing an earlier document — would have updated the numbers to reflect later demographics rather than just copying the source. The text does not claim to be updating. It claims to be transmitting.

Williamson, Blenkinsopp, and Klein all read these single-digit discrepancies as ordinary scribal slips in numerical transmission. Hebrew numbers written out as words are still vulnerable when a scribe is working from a damaged exemplar or from dictation, and the units position is the most error-prone slot in any numeral. The 666/667 split is almost certainly one of those slips, not a theological signal and not a demographic event.

The interesting thing about the 666 figure is its later afterlife — popular apocalyptic readers from the medieval period through modern dispensationalists have occasionally read Adonikam's number as somehow significant given Revelation 13:18. That is a fun coincidence and nothing more, since 1 Esdras 5:14 reads 667 (agreeing with Nehemiah against Ezra) and the wider list shows the same kind of numerical instability across MT, LXX, and the 1 Esdras tradition. Coincidence theology built on a textually unstable number is a house built on sand.
scholarship: H. G. M. Williamson, Ezra, Nehemiah, Word Biblical Commentary 16 (Word Books, 1985), pp. 28-32.
Joseph Blenkinsopp, Ezra-Nehemiah: A Commentary, Old Testament Library (Westminster John Knox, 1988), pp. 83-87.
Ralph W. Klein, 'Ezra-Nehemiah, Books of,' in The Anchor Bible Dictionary, Vol. 2, ed. David Noel Freedman (Doubleday, 1992), pp. 731-742.
Gleason L. Archer, Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties (Zondervan, 1982), pp. 229-232.
Loring W. Batten, A Critical and Exegetical Commentary on the Books of Ezra and Nehemiah, International Critical Commentary (T&T Clark, 1913), pp. 80-85.

contradictions.question: How many of Bigvai's offspring returned from Babylon?
contradictions.summary: Ezra 2:14 counts 2,056 children of Bigvai returning from Babylon. Nehemiah 7:19, working from the same returnee registry, gives 2,067. Eleven-person gap in numbers that both texts claim to be transmitting from a common source.
contradictions.commentary:
Yet another data point in the Ezra 2 versus Nehemiah 7 numerical disagreement. By the time we get to Bigvai in the roster, the pattern is unmistakable — these are two transmissions of one document that have drifted from each other in dozens of places. The Bigvai discrepancy of eleven is in the same ballpark as several other entries and points to the same mechanism: scribal slippage in numerical material across two centuries of independent copying.

Williamson and Blenkinsopp both emphasize that the units and tens digits in Hebrew numerals are the most vulnerable spots in any roster, because they carry no semantic constraint that would help a scribe catch a transposition. Compare this to a verb or a name, where surrounding context constrains the possible readings. A number has no such redundancy. You write 'fifty-six' and you write 'sixty-seven' and there is no internal check that flags the slip if you misread your exemplar. This is exactly how textual data fails, and we see the same pattern in the LXX-versus-MT divergences for Genesis 5 patriarch ages and the Saul-age numbers in 1 Samuel 13:1.

The apologetic response runs through the standard playbook — one list was taken before the journey, the other after; some people were counted under different family heads; the records reflect different counting conventions. None of these survive scrutiny because the discrepancies do not pattern in any directional way that would support a demographic explanation. Some families gain, others lose, and the gains and losses are not correlated with anything in the surrounding text. That is what random scribal drift looks like, not what intentional demographic updating looks like.

The most honest position on the Bigvai numbers and the rest of the Ezra 2/Nehemiah 7 divergences is the one critical scholarship has held for over a century: these are paired transmissions of a common source, and the numerical data has corrupted in at least one stream and possibly both. The doctrine of inerrant transmission cannot survive that, and the doctrine of inspired original autographs only survives if you concede that we do not have access to those autographs in the form of the texts we actually possess. Take your pick.
scholarship: H. G. M. Williamson, Ezra, Nehemiah, Word Biblical Commentary 16 (Word Books, 1985), pp. 28-32.
Joseph Blenkinsopp, Ezra-Nehemiah: A Commentary, Old Testament Library (Westminster John Knox, 1988), pp. 83-87.
Sara Japhet, From the Rivers of Babylon to the Highlands of Judah: Collected Studies on the Restoration Period (Eisenbrauns, 2006), pp. 366-372.
Jacob M. Myers, Ezra, Nehemiah, Anchor Bible 14 (Doubleday, 1965), pp. 14-18.
Emanuel Tov, Textual Criticism of the Hebrew Bible, 3rd ed. (Fortress, 2012), pp. 11-13.

contradictions.question: How many of Adin's offspring returned from Babylon?
contradictions.summary: Ezra 2:15 lists 454 returnees from the family of Adin. Nehemiah 7:20 gives 655 for the same family in the same registry. The gap is 201 people in a single family entry.
contradictions.commentary:
The Adin discrepancy is one of the larger ones in the Ezra/Nehemiah parallel, and like the Azgad case it sits squarely outside any plausible demographic explanation. You do not gain or lose 201 people from a single family by ordinary attrition or recruitment between two records of the same returnee group. What you do get is a scribal slip in the hundreds digit — the difference between 'four hundred' (arba meot) and 'six hundred' (shesh meot) in Hebrew is exactly the kind of thing that can be misread or miscopied, especially from a damaged or worn exemplar.

Williamson notes in WBC 16 that the Adin number is one of the entries where the textual evidence makes scribal corruption almost inescapable as the explanation. 1 Esdras 5:14 reads 454 for the Adin family (Adinu in the Greek text), agreeing with Ezra against Nehemiah, which makes the Nehemiah 655 the outlier of the three witnesses. That kind of two-against-one split is exactly what textual critics use to triangulate the original reading — when two independent witnesses converge and one diverges by 201, the diverging witness is the likely site of scribal corruption.

The apologetic move here is sometimes to suggest that the lists count different categories — Ezra counting heads of household and Nehemiah counting all family members, or one counting men and the other counting families. That falls apart immediately because both texts use identical formulaic language ('the children of Adin, X hundred and Y'), and neither text gives any indication that the categories of counting differ. You would have to import that distinction from outside the text, which is exactly the kind of ad hoc move that gives apologetic harmonization its bad reputation.

The critical conclusion is that these two transmissions of a common returnee registry have corrupted in at least one place — almost certainly in the Adin entry — and the original number is not recoverable from the surviving witnesses. That is a perfectly normal textual outcome for ancient numerical material. It is not a problem for the historical reality of the return, but it is a problem for any doctrine of inerrant transmission. The verdict is corruption, not contradiction in the divine source.
scholarship: H. G. M. Williamson, Ezra, Nehemiah, Word Biblical Commentary 16 (Word Books, 1985), pp. 28-32.
Joseph Blenkinsopp, Ezra-Nehemiah: A Commentary, Old Testament Library (Westminster John Knox, 1988), pp. 83-87.
Loring W. Batten, A Critical and Exegetical Commentary on the Books of Ezra and Nehemiah, International Critical Commentary (T&T Clark, 1913), pp. 80-85.
Zipora Talshir, I Esdras: From Origin to Translation, SBL Septuagint and Cognate Studies 47 (Society of Biblical Literature, 1999), pp. 246-251.
Jacob M. Myers, Ezra, Nehemiah, Anchor Bible 14 (Doubleday, 1965), pp. 14-18.

The children of Adin, six hundred fifty and five. Nehemiah 7:20

contradictions.question: How many of Bezai's offspring returned from Babylon?
contradictions.summary: Ezra 2:17 has 323 children of Bezai returning. Nehemiah 7:23, copying the same returnee registry, gives 324. One-person discrepancy in a list that both texts claim to be transmitting from a single source document.
contradictions.commentary:
By this point in the roster, the picture is fully formed — every few family entries in Ezra 2 disagrees with its Nehemiah 7 counterpart by some amount, sometimes by one person, sometimes by hundreds, sometimes by more than a thousand. The Bezai case sits at the low end of the spectrum and looks like exactly the kind of single-digit transposition that scribes routinely commit when copying numerical material.

The apologist defense for single-digit gaps is the easiest one to mount — 'someone died,' 'someone changed their mind,' 'a count was off by one.' Archer leans on variants of this in his Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties. The problem is not that any individual single-digit explanation is implausible. The problem is that the explanation has to be deployed dozens of times across the chapter, alongside cases where the demographic-update theory simply cannot account for the gap (see Azgad, Adin). At some point you have to pick a mechanism that explains the whole pattern rather than patching each verse with a different ad hoc rescue.

The scribal-transmission explanation accounts for the whole pattern. Single-digit slips, hundreds-digit slips, thousands-digit slips, and even patriarch-name spelling drift (Bani versus Binnui in id 321) all flow naturally from the model that two copies of a common source have drifted from each other over centuries of independent transmission. The demographic-update model has to argue that the original recorder made the updates only for the variant cases and not for the ones where the numbers match, which is exactly the kind of explanation that has no independent support in the text.

Blenkinsopp in OTL and Williamson in WBC 16 both treat this whole class of Ezra/Nehemiah numerical disagreements as textual rather than historical. They are agnostic on the original totals because the witnesses cannot be reconciled, and they are clear that the source-copying language in Nehemiah 7:5 rules out the demographic-update theory. The verdict in the academic literature has been stable for over a century. Inerrancy needs a different model. Critical scholarship already has one.
scholarship: H. G. M. Williamson, Ezra, Nehemiah, Word Biblical Commentary 16 (Word Books, 1985), pp. 28-32.
Joseph Blenkinsopp, Ezra-Nehemiah: A Commentary, Old Testament Library (Westminster John Knox, 1988), pp. 83-87.
Gleason L. Archer, Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties (Zondervan, 1982), pp. 229-232.

Jacob M. Myers, Ezra, Nehemiah, Anchor Bible 14 (Doubleday, 1965), pp. 14-18.

The children of Bezai, three hundred twenty and four. Nehemiah 7:23

contradictions.question: How many of Bethlehem and Netophah's offspring returned from Babylon?
contradictions.summary: Ezra 2:21-22 separates the figures and gives 123 men of Bethlehem and 56 men of Netophah, for a combined total of 179. Nehemiah 7:26 collapses the two locations into one entry and gives 188 men of Bethlehem and Netophah combined. The totals differ by nine, and the formatting of the two entries diverges as well.
contradictions.commentary:
The Bethlehem/Netophah entry is one of the more diagnostic cases in the Ezra 2 / Nehemiah 7 parallel, because it is not just the numbers that differ — the structural formatting differs. Ezra 2 treats Bethlehem and Netophah as two separate locations with two separate totals (123 + 56 = 179). Nehemiah 7 combines them into a single line item with a single combined total (188). This is exactly the kind of editorial intervention that gives away the hand of a transmitting scribe rather than the hand of an inspired original.

The apologist move here is to argue that the totals are compatible if some people moved between censuses, or that the combined figure in Nehemiah includes outlying villages around Bethlehem that Ezra separates out under Netophah. That sort of harmonization is unfalsifiable — you can always invent a category that absorbs the gap — but it is not what the text actually says. The text in Ezra is precise: 123 men of Bethlehem, 56 men of Netophah. The text in Nehemiah is also precise: 188 men of Bethlehem and Netophah combined. Neither text mentions a third location, and there is no internal evidence that either author understood the categories differently.

Williamson in WBC 16 reads this as a clear case of editorial reformatting in one of the two transmissions, with the numerical gap reflecting either a scribal slip or a difference in how the two editors handled the boundaries of the geographical categories. Blenkinsopp concurs. The 1 Esdras 5 parallel here is also revealing — the Greek text preserves yet a third arithmetic, with 1 Esdras 5:17-18 giving Bethlehem (Bethlomon) 123 and Netophah (Netophas) 55 for a combined total of 178, distinct from both Ezra's 179 and Nehemiah's 188. That is the third strike against the idea that we have access to a single stable original number.

What this case shows particularly clearly is that the two transmissions are not just numerically divergent but structurally divergent. The editor of Nehemiah 7 felt free to collapse two location entries into one. That kind of editorial latitude in supposedly identical material is exactly what we would expect from human transmission and exactly what we would not expect if both books were preserving a single divinely inspired register without modification. The verdict here is not just textual drift but visible editorial intervention.
scholarship: H. G. M. Williamson, Ezra, Nehemiah, Word Biblical Commentary 16 (Word Books, 1985), pp. 28-32.
Joseph Blenkinsopp, Ezra-Nehemiah: A Commentary, Old Testament Library (Westminster John Knox, 1988), pp. 83-87.
Sara Japhet, From the Rivers of Babylon to the Highlands of Judah: Collected Studies on the Restoration Period (Eisenbrauns, 2006), pp. 366-372.
Lester L. Grabbe, A History of the Jews and Judaism in the Second Temple Period, Vol. 1: Yehud (T&T Clark, 2004), pp. 285-291.
Loring W. Batten, A Critical and Exegetical Commentary on the Books of Ezra and Nehemiah, International Critical Commentary (T&T Clark, 1913), pp. 85-89.

contradictions.question: How many of Lod, Hadid, and Ono's offspring returned from Babylon?
contradictions.summary: Ezra 2:33 counts 725 returnees from Lod, Hadid, and Ono. Nehemiah 7:37, transmitting the same returnee list, gives 721. Four-person gap in a list that both texts claim to be reproducing from the same source.
contradictions.commentary:
The Lod/Hadid/Ono entry is one of the cases where the demographic-update apologetic looks most plausible at first glance — a four-person gap could easily be attributed to a few people dying or a few stragglers joining late. The problem is that the explanation has to be deployed dozens of times across the chapter, sometimes for one-person gaps, sometimes for thousand-person gaps, and at no point does the text itself signal that this is what is happening. Nehemiah 7:5 says the chapter is reproducing the original returnee registry, not updating it.

What makes this case interesting is that 1 Esdras 5:22 — the Greek third witness to the same registry — gives 725 here, agreeing with Ezra against Nehemiah. That kind of two-against-one split is exactly what textual critics use to triangulate the original reading. When two witnesses agree and one disagrees, the disagreeing witness is the likely site of scribal corruption, all things being equal. In this case, the corruption is probably in the Nehemiah 7 transmission rather than the Ezra 2 transmission, but the point is that we can only make that judgment by treating the texts as ordinary human documents whose transmission has to be reconstructed, not as inerrant divine deposits whose every word stands.

Talshir's monograph on 1 Esdras is the standard treatment of these triangulations, and her work shows that for many of the Ezra 2 / Nehemiah 7 discrepancies the 1 Esdras evidence allows reasonably confident reconstruction of the original numbers. That is good news for historical reconstruction of the post-exilic returnee community. It is bad news for inerrancy, because the methodology Talshir uses depends on treating the biblical witnesses as fallible and reconstructible rather than as perfectly preserved.

The apologist defense of choice — that all three numbers are simultaneously correct because they reflect different snapshots — has to invent demographic mechanisms that the text never describes, and it has to do so dozens of times. The critical alternative — that the original list had one number, two transmissions copied it imperfectly, and a third transmission preserved a different reading — has a coherent mechanism and matches the manuscript evidence. One model has a mechanism. The other has a problem.
scholarship: H. G. M. Williamson, Ezra, Nehemiah, Word Biblical Commentary 16 (Word Books, 1985), pp. 28-32.
Zipora Talshir, I Esdras: From Origin to Translation, SBL Septuagint and Cognate Studies 47 (Society of Biblical Literature, 1999), pp. 246-251.

Jacob M. Myers, Ezra, Nehemiah, Anchor Bible 14 (Doubleday, 1965), pp. 14-18.
Emanuel Tov, Textual Criticism of the Hebrew Bible, 3rd ed. (Fortress, 2012), pp. 11-13.

contradictions.question: How many of Senaah's offspring returned from Babylon?
contradictions.summary: Ezra 2:35 lists 3,630 returnees from Senaah. Nehemiah 7:38, transmitting the same returnee registry, gives 3,930. Three-hundred-person discrepancy in a single entry.
contradictions.commentary:
The Senaah figure is one of the larger gaps in the Ezra 2 / Nehemiah 7 family roster and it shows the same pattern as Azgad and Adin — the difference is too large for any demographic-update theory to absorb. Three hundred people do not appear or disappear from a single family between two near-contemporary records of the same event without some textual explanation. The text does not provide one, which means the explanation has to come from scribal transmission.

The hundreds digit in Hebrew numerals is one of the easier slots to miscopy, and the difference between 'six hundred' (shesh meot) and 'nine hundred' (tesha meot) is exactly the kind of slip that can happen if the exemplar is damaged or if the scribe is working from dictation. Williamson and Blenkinsopp both flag the Senaah number as one of the entries where transmission corruption is the only plausible explanation for the gap. 1 Esdras 5:23 gives 3,330 (against Ezra's 3,630 and Nehemiah's 3,930), which is yet a third number and reinforces the diagnosis.

What is interesting about the Senaah entry specifically is that it is unusually large — over three thousand people from a single 'family' is more than ten times the size of most of the other entries in the list. Some commentators have suggested that 'Senaah' may not be a family name at all but a place name or even a generic term, which would account for the large number but would also mean that Ezra 2 and Nehemiah 7 may not be counting the same thing in the same way. That is a respectable scholarly suggestion but it does not rescue the inerrancy reading — it just adds a layer of editorial divergence on top of the numerical one.

The critical-scholarship verdict on Senaah is the same as on the rest of the roster — these are paired transmissions of a common source, and the numerical data has corrupted in at least one stream. The honest read is that the original number is not recoverable from the surviving witnesses, and treating the discrepancy as a theological signal rather than a textual problem is exactly the kind of post-hoc rationalization that inerrantist hermeneutics has to deploy to keep the doctrine intact. Take your pick — coherent mechanism or doctrinal patchwork.

contradictions.question: How many of Asaph's offspring returned from Babylon?
contradictions.summary: Ezra 2:41 reports 128 singers from the family of Asaph among the returnees. Nehemiah 7:44, reproducing the same registry, gives 148. Twenty-person gap in a single Levitical entry that both texts claim to be transmitting from a common source.
contradictions.commentary:
The Asaph entry is interesting because it sits inside the Levitical and cultic personnel section of the returnee roster, which is the part of the list where you might most expect the editors to have updated the numbers — these are the people who staffed the rebuilt temple, and the numbers had ongoing administrative relevance. So if the demographic-update theory were ever going to work, it would work here. And yet the actual text does not signal an update; both Ezra 2 and Nehemiah 7 frame their respective lists as transmissions of the original returnee count.

The 128/148 split is exactly the kind of mid-range gap that is hardest to attribute to either a single-digit scribal slip or a hundreds-digit miscopy. Twenty people. Some commentators have suggested that the discrepancy could reflect different cutoffs for who counted as an Asaphite singer — perhaps including or excluding apprentices, or counting heads of guild versus all members. That kind of category-shift explanation has more traction here than it does for the family entries, because the singers were a professional guild with possibly fuzzy membership criteria. But the texts do not specify any such category distinction, and the harmonization remains speculation.

Williamson in WBC 16 notes that the Levitical and singer numbers across Ezra 2 and Nehemiah 7 are particularly unstable in the manuscript tradition. 1 Esdras 5:27 reads 128 (agreeing with Ezra) in the main text with a manuscript variant of 148 (agreeing with Nehemiah), showing that the singer figure was actively oscillating across the Greek transmission as well. That kind of textual instability points to the same conclusion as the rest of the roster — the numbers are textually corrupt and the original cannot be recovered with confidence.

For the inerrantist, the Asaph discrepancy is one of the easier cases to spin because the category-shift explanation has some plausibility. For the critical scholar, the case still illustrates the same pattern that runs through the entire chapter: paired transmissions of a common source, with numerical divergences that cannot all be rescued by ad hoc demographic or category-based explanations. The most parsimonious read is scribal corruption, and the doctrine that requires every transmitted number to be inerrant has to keep paying tolls every time it crosses this bridge.

contradictions.question: How many children of the porters returned from Babylon?
contradictions.summary: Ezra 2:42 totals 139 returnees among the porters (gatekeepers) from six named families. Nehemiah 7:45 lists the same six family names and gives 138. One-person gap in a list of porters whose composition is identical in both texts.
contradictions.commentary:
The porters entry is a clean diagnostic case because both Ezra 2:42 and Nehemiah 7:45 name exactly the same six gatekeeper families in the same order — Shallum, Ater, Talmon, Akkub, Hatita, Shobai — but disagree on the total by one person. There is no editorial reformatting, no category drift, no question about whether the texts are counting the same group. They are counting the same group. They disagree by one.

This is exactly the diagnostic profile for a scribal slip in the units digit of the total. Both texts agree on the constituents but disagree on the sum. Either one scribe miscopied the total or one scribe (or compiler) tallied the family numbers independently and got a slightly different answer than the source document. Williamson and Blenkinsopp both treat this entry as a textbook case of low-level numerical corruption in transmission.

The apologetic move on a single-digit gap is usually to argue that someone died en route or someone joined late, but the porters case undercuts that defense because the family-by-family composition is identical. There is no room for someone to have joined or left a specific family without showing up in the family-level totals, and the family-level totals are not given in either text — only the grand total of 139 versus 138. So the divergence sits exclusively in the summation, which is exactly where you would expect a scribal slip to occur.

The critical-scholarship verdict on this entry is uncontroversial: this is textual drift in a single arithmetic step, the kind of thing that happens routinely when ancient scribes copy numerical lists. It does not bear any theological weight, and it does not require any clever historical reconstruction. It just requires the admission that the transmitted text contains arithmetic errors. For the inerrantist that admission is the entire problem; for everyone else it is unremarkable.

contradictions.question: How many of Delaiah, Tobiah, and Nekoda's offspring returned from Babylon?
contradictions.summary: Ezra 2:60 reports 652 returnees from the joint families of Delaiah, Tobiah, and Nekoda — a group flagged as unable to prove their Israelite descent. Nehemiah 7:62, transmitting the same registry, gives 642. Ten-person discrepancy in a single combined entry.
contradictions.commentary:
The Delaiah/Tobiah/Nekoda entry is particularly interesting because of its context — these are the families that, according to both Ezra and Nehemiah, could not produce documentation of their Israelite ancestry and whose status as part of the returnee community was therefore disputed. The fact that both texts flag this group identically but then give different totals for them shows that the editorial framing was stable across transmission while the numerical data drifted.

The ten-person gap is the kind of mid-range divergence that the demographic-update theory has the most trouble with. It is too large for a one-person attrition explanation and too small for the hundreds-digit miscopy explanation. The most plausible scribal mechanism is a tens-digit transposition — confusing the Hebrew written-out forms of 'fifty' (chamishshim) and 'forty' (arba'im) — which is a routine slip in the manuscript tradition. Williamson and Blenkinsopp both treat this as the likely diagnosis.

The theological framing of this group is identical in both texts: these are the families whose claim to Israelite descent was challenged, and who were therefore in a liminal category within the returnee community. Some commentators have argued that the numerical instability here reflects ongoing dispute about who belonged and who did not, with different scribes including or excluding different sub-groups based on their assessment of the genealogical claims. That is a respectable suggestion, but it falls into the same category-shift category as the Asaphite singers — it is plausible speculation, but the text does not signal it explicitly.

The critical conclusion remains the same as for the rest of the roster: paired transmissions of a common source, with numerical divergence consistent with scribal slippage. The Delaiah/Tobiah/Nekoda entry adds the interesting wrinkle that the disputed-ancestry framing was preserved stably while the numbers were not, which is exactly the pattern you would expect from human transmission — the prose is more redundant and harder to corrupt than the numerals. One model has an explanation. The other has a problem.

contradictions.question: How many singing men and women returned from Babylon?
contradictions.summary: Ezra 2:65 reports 200 singing men and women among the returnees. Nehemiah 7:67, transmitting the same registry, gives 245. Forty-five-person gap in a single category that both texts claim to be reproducing from a common source.
contradictions.commentary:
The singing men and women entry is a clean parallel to the Asaph singers case earlier in the roster, but with a substantially larger gap — 45 people rather than 20. The two entries are not the same. The Asaph entry counts the temple singers specifically, while this entry counts general male and female singers among the household staff of the returnees, a different category of personnel altogether. Both, however, are professional or quasi-professional categories where membership criteria may have been fuzzy.

The 200/245 split is large enough to make the demographic-update theory difficult to sustain. Forty-five people is not the kind of gap you get from ordinary attrition between two near-contemporary records. The scribal mechanism is harder to pin to a single slot than for the family entries — this could be a tens-digit corruption (200 versus 240, with units digit drift on top) or it could reflect a genuine editorial intervention in one of the transmissions, where one editor included a category of personnel that another editor excluded.

Williamson notes in WBC 16 that the singer numbers in particular are unstable across the textual witnesses, with 1 Esdras 5:42 reading 245 (agreeing with Nehemiah against Ezra). The agreement of 1 Esdras with Nehemiah here is the reverse of what we saw for the Lod/Hadid/Ono entry, where 1 Esdras agreed with Ezra against Nehemiah. The witnesses do not cluster cleanly across the chapter as a whole, which is exactly what we would expect from a textual tradition where multiple independent corruptions have accumulated rather than a clean two-branch divergence.

The critical conclusion is the same as for the rest of the roster — the numerical data in the Ezra 2 / Nehemiah 7 parallel is not stable across the manuscript tradition, and the original figures cannot be reconstructed with confidence from the surviving witnesses. The apologist needs both totals to be correct simultaneously, which requires inventing demographic mechanisms the text does not describe. The critical scholar just needs the texts to be human documents that drifted in transmission, which is what the manuscript evidence shows. One model fits the data. The other fights it.

contradictions.question: How much gold, silver, and clothing did the people give?
contradictions.summary: Ezra 2:69 records the returnees' contribution to the temple treasury as 61,000 drams of gold, 5,000 pounds of silver, and 100 priests' garments. Nehemiah 7:72, transmitting the same registry, gives 20,000 drams of gold, 2,000 pounds of silver, and 67 priests' garments. Three separate categories of donation, three separate disagreements, in a single ledger entry that both texts claim to be reproducing from a common source.
contradictions.commentary:
This is the climactic divergence in the Ezra 2 / Nehemiah 7 parallel and it cannot be rescued by any of the standard harmonizations. The discrepancies in the family rosters might be argued away one by one by appeal to scribal slips or demographic updates, but the donation ledger disagrees across three separate categories simultaneously — gold, silver, and priestly garments — and the disagreements are large in every category. Sixty-one thousand drams versus twenty thousand. Five thousand pounds versus two thousand. One hundred garments versus sixty-seven.

The apologetic playbook here gets really creative. One move is to argue that Ezra 2 records the total contribution while Nehemiah 7 records only the contribution of the laity, with the priests and Levites contributing separately and Nehemiah omitting their share. This is essentially the position taken by Archer in his Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties. The problem is that the text of Nehemiah 7:70-72 actually does break down the contributions by donor category (the governor, the heads of the fathers, and the rest of the people) and the sum of those breakdowns still does not produce the Ezra 2 total. So the rescue requires further patching.

Williamson in WBC 16 reads this as one of the clearest cases of full-blown editorial intervention in one of the two transmissions. The Nehemiah 7 ledger has been reorganized to break down the donations by donor category, and in the process the numbers have either been altered, corrupted, or were never the same as Ezra 2 to begin with. Blenkinsopp concurs and adds that the dram counts in particular are suspect because the unit of measurement (the daric) is anachronistic to the period of the original return, which suggests that at least one of the editors has updated the figures to reflect a later currency standard. That kind of editorial updating is exactly what we would expect from human transmission and exactly what we would not expect from divinely inspired identical reproduction.

The critical verdict here is that the donation ledger is the strongest single case in the entire chapter for editorial intervention in transmission. The numbers are not just numerically different — they are categorically restructured in ways that no demographic-update theory can absorb. The apologist needs all three totals in all three categories to be simultaneously correct. The critical scholar just needs editorial reorganization across two centuries of transmission. One position has a mechanism that fits the evidence. The other is paying compound tolls. Take your pick.

contradictions.question: Was Zechariah Iddo's son or grandson?
contradictions.summary: Ezra 5:1 and Ezra 6:14 call the prophet Zechariah 'the son of Iddo.' Zechariah 1:1 calls him 'the son of Berechiah, the son of Iddo,' which makes Iddo his grandfather and Berechiah his father. The two genealogies cannot both be literal son-of relationships.
contradictions.commentary:
The Zechariah genealogy is one of the cleaner contradictions in the Hebrew Bible because the texts disagree about a single biographical fact in language that is structurally identical. Ezra says Zechariah is 'the son of Iddo' (ben Iddo). Zechariah's own book opens by calling him 'the son of Berechiah, the son of Iddo' (ben Berechiah ben Iddo). If the Zechariah 1:1 genealogy is right, the Ezra references are skipping a generation. If the Ezra references are right, the Zechariah 1:1 genealogy is inventing one.

The standard apologetic harmonization is to argue that the Hebrew word ben does not strictly mean 'son' but can also mean 'descendant' in a more general sense. This is true as a lexical observation — ben is used in extended genealogies to skip generations, as in 'Jesus, the son of David, the son of Abraham' in Matthew 1:1. So the Ezra references could be read as 'Zechariah, the descendant of Iddo,' skipping over the intermediate Berechiah. This is the position taken by Archer and by most conservative commentators. The harmonization is grammatically possible, but it has costs.

The cost is that the same word ben is being used to mean two different things in two adjacent biblical texts about the same person, with no internal signal to tell the reader which sense is operative. And the Zechariah 1:1 formulation 'ben Berechiah ben Iddo' uses ben twice in a single sentence, which strongly suggests that the author intended literal father-son chains rather than generalized descent. Critical scholarship from Petersen's OTL volume to Meyers and Meyers in the Anchor Bible reads Zechariah 1:1 as a literal three-generation genealogy and treats the Ezra references as either compressed shorthand or as preserving a different tradition about Zechariah's lineage.

There is a more interesting complicating factor here, which is that the name 'Berechiah' may have been imported into the prophetic tradition from a separate figure — Isaiah 8:2 mentions a Zechariah son of Jeberechiah (a longer theophoric variant of the same name) as a witness in Isaiah's prophetic activity, more than two centuries before the postexilic prophet. Jesus famously conflates these two Zechariahs in Matthew 23:35 when he refers to 'Zechariah son of Berechiah whom you murdered between the temple and the altar,' applying the temple-murder narrative of 2 Chronicles 24:20-22 (which is about Zechariah son of Jehoiada) to the wrong Zechariah. The textual record around 'Zechariah son of Berechiah' is messy across multiple biblical books, and the Ezra/Zechariah genealogy disagreement is part of that broader tangle. The honest verdict is that we have at least two distinct traditions about the prophet's lineage and the texts do not cleanly harmonize.

contradictions.question: Is the devil tied up or free to roam?
contradictions.summary: 2 Peter 2:4 says the rebellious angels were cast into hell and bound in chains of darkness, and Jude 6 repeats that the angels who left their proper estate are kept in everlasting chains under darkness. Job 1:7, Job 2:2, and 1 Peter 5:8 describe Satan as actively walking the earth — going to and fro, prowling like a lion seeking whom he may devour. The biblical witness on the location and status of the devil is not internally consistent.
contradictions.commentary:
This contradiction works because the New Testament and Old Testament texts in question are operating with completely different cosmologies and timelines for the satanic figure. Job's adversary (ha-satan, 'the adversary') is part of the divine council, a heavenly prosecutor who roams the earth observing humanity and reporting back to God. He is not a fallen rebel; he is a functionary. The 2 Peter / Jude framework, by contrast, draws on Second Temple Jewish apocalyptic literature — particularly 1 Enoch and the Book of Watchers — where rebellious angels were imprisoned in chains awaiting final judgment. These are two different traditions about supernatural opposition figures and they have been merged uncomfortably in the Christian canon.

The apologetic move here is usually to argue that 'the devil' and 'the angels that sinned' are different entities. The 2 Peter and Jude references, on this reading, are about the imprisoned watchers from 1 Enoch — the angels who came down and fathered the Nephilim in Genesis 6 — and not about Satan personally. Satan remains free to roam (per Job and 1 Peter) while his angelic cohort is in chains awaiting judgment. This is the position taken by most conservative commentators, including Bauckham in his WBC volume on Jude and 2 Peter, who carefully distinguishes the Enochic watcher tradition from the satanic-prince tradition.

The harmonization has real merit at the level of Second Temple background, because Bauckham is correct that 2 Peter 2:4 and Jude 6 are drawing on the Enochic watcher tradition specifically. The problem is that the harmonization requires the reader to import a distinction between 'the devil' and 'the angels that sinned' that is not present in mainstream Christian theology and is actively contradicted by texts like Revelation 12:9, which identifies the devil with 'the great dragon' who led 'his angels' in rebellion. Once Revelation collapses the satanic figure together with the rebellious angelic host, the watcher tradition and the satan tradition become a single narrative — and that single narrative has Satan both bound (per 2 Peter/Jude) and free (per Job/1 Peter) simultaneously.

The more honest critical position is that the biblical texts preserve multiple, incompatible traditions about supernatural opposition figures, and the post-canonical Christian tradition flattens them into a single 'Satan' character whose behavior is then inconsistent because the source materials were always inconsistent. Job's adversary is not Jude's chained watcher is not Revelation's dragon. They have been theologically merged but they were never originally the same character. The contradiction is real and it is a feature of how the canon was assembled, not a problem that careful exegesis can dissolve.

contradictions.question: Does God destroy both the righteous and the wicked?
contradictions.summary: Job 9:22 says God destroys both the perfect and the wicked. Ecclesiastes 7:15 observes the righteous perishing in their righteousness while the wicked prolong their lives. Ezekiel 21:3 has God promising to cut off both the righteous and the wicked from a land. Against this, Ezekiel 18:8-9, 18:19-20, and 33:18-19 insist that the righteous shall live and the wicked shall die — strict moral retribution. The Hebrew Bible contains both views and they do not reconcile.
contradictions.commentary:
This is one of the cleanest internal-tension cases in the Hebrew Bible because the contradiction sits inside the same book (Ezekiel) and the broader contradiction maps onto a recognized tension in ancient Israelite theology between covenantal retribution and the empirical observation that righteous people often suffer while wicked people often prosper. The Deuteronomistic framework promises that obedience produces blessing and disobedience produces curse. Job and Ecclesiastes are extended wisdom-literature meditations on the failure of that framework in actual experience. Ezekiel sits in the middle, articulating both views in different chapters depending on the rhetorical purpose of the oracle.

The apologetic harmonization here is usually to argue that Job 9:22 and Ecclesiastes 7:15 are 'observational' rather than 'doctrinal' — Job and Qoheleth are reporting how things appear from human perspective, while Ezekiel 18 and 33 are stating God's actual policy of moral retribution. The Ezekiel 21:3 passage gets harmonized as a specific judgment oracle against a specific group at a specific historical moment (the Babylonian destruction), rather than a general policy statement. This is essentially the position of evangelical commentators like Block in his NICOT volume on Ezekiel.

The problem with the observational-versus-doctrinal harmonization is that Job is presented in the canonical framework as a divinely-inspired text and Job 9:22 is spoken by Job himself, who is explicitly affirmed by God at the end of the book as having spoken what is right (Job 42:7) in contrast to the friends who defended the conventional doctrine of retribution. So the canonical framing of Job actually validates Job 9:22 as theologically correct rather than treating it as merely human misperception. The same applies to Ecclesiastes — the canonical framing treats Qoheleth as a wisdom teacher whose observations are authoritative, not as a complainer whose perceptions need correcting.

The critical conclusion is that the Hebrew Bible preserves competing theological frameworks for understanding suffering and prosperity, and the contradictions are not resolvable by appeal to differences in genre or rhetorical purpose. Job, Ecclesiastes, and parts of Ezekiel reflect a wisdom tradition that took seriously the empirical failure of strict retribution. Ezekiel 18 and 33 and the Deuteronomistic tradition more broadly defended retribution as God's actual policy. Both traditions are in the canon and they are not the same theology. The honest read is that the canon is theologically pluralistic on this question, not that careful exegesis makes the tension go away.

contradictions.question: Can God be found through reason alone?
contradictions.summary: Romans 1:20 says God's invisible attributes — his eternal power and divine nature — are clearly perceived from the things that have been made, leaving humans without excuse. Job 11:7 asks rhetorically whether anyone can find out God by searching, and the implied answer is no. Paul says natural revelation makes God knowable through reason; Job's friend Zophar says it doesn't.
contradictions.commentary:
This contradiction operates at the level of natural theology — the question of whether unaided human reason, working from the evidence of the natural world, can arrive at reliable knowledge of God. Paul in Romans 1:20 is making a foundational claim that the answer is yes: the created order itself reveals enough about God's existence and attributes that pagans who fail to acknowledge him are 'without excuse.' This single verse has been the basis for an enormous chunk of Christian apologetic argumentation, from Aquinas's natural-theology project to William Paley's design argument to modern intelligent-design literature. Job 11:7 sits in considerable tension with all of that.

The standard apologetic move is to argue that Job 11:7 is spoken by Zophar, one of Job's three friends, and that the canonical framing of Job is critical of the friends' theology. Zophar at the end of the book is rebuked along with the other friends for not speaking what is right about God (Job 42:7), so the apologist can argue that his rhetorical question — 'Can you find out God by searching?' — is not authoritative scripture in the same sense that Romans 1:20 is. This is the position taken by most evangelical commentators, including Walton in his NIVAC volume on Job.

The harmonization has some force but it does not fully work, because Zophar's claim that God cannot be found out by human searching is consistent with what God himself says from the whirlwind in Job 38-41. The divine speeches are an extended argument that human understanding is utterly inadequate to grasp the divine perspective. Job, who has been searching for understanding throughout the book, ends up acknowledging in Job 42:3 that he has spoken of things too wonderful for him that he did not know. The book of Job as a whole is therefore not friendly to the Pauline claim that God's nature is clearly visible from creation — quite the opposite, the book argues that creation reveals enough about God's power to silence human protest but not enough to allow human reason to arrive at theological conclusions.

The critical conclusion is that the Hebrew Bible and the Pauline corpus represent two different theological traditions on the question of natural revelation. Job, parts of Ecclesiastes, and much of the wisdom tradition are skeptical about the capacity of human reason to access reliable theological knowledge. Romans 1:20 and the Pauline tradition more broadly take the opposite position. The contradiction is structural and reflects a real divergence between two streams of biblical theology, not a misreading of either text. Take your pick — natural theology that works, or wisdom skepticism that doesn't trust it. The Bible has both.

contradictions.question: Do evildoers prosper?
contradictions.summary: Job 12:6 says the tents of robbers prosper and those who provoke God are secure. Psalm 73:3-7, 12 describes the prosperity of the wicked at length — they are not in trouble, they wear pride as a necklace, they increase in riches. Jeremiah 12:1 asks why the way of the wicked prospers. Against this, Psalm 34:21 says evil shall slay the wicked and those who hate the righteous shall be desolate. The biblical wisdom and poetic tradition contains both empirical observations that evil prospers and theological assertions that it does not.
contradictions.commentary:
This is the same theological tension that runs through the previous entry on whether God destroys the righteous along with the wicked, but with a different rhetorical framing. The question of whether evildoers prosper is the empirical question; the question of whether they should is the theological one. The Hebrew Bible repeatedly notices that the empirical answer is yes — Job, Psalm 73, and Jeremiah 12 all describe the prosperity of the wicked as an observable fact that creates a theological problem for those who hold to the doctrine of strict retribution. Psalm 34:21 represents the doctrinal counter-claim that the empirical observation is wrong or temporary.

The apologetic harmonization here is usually a long-term-versus-short-term distinction. The wicked prosper now, but they will be desolate eventually — whether in this life through eventual divine judgment or in the next life through final judgment. This is the position taken by Kidner in his Tyndale Old Testament Commentary on Psalms and by most evangelical readers of the wisdom literature. On this reading, Job 12, Psalm 73, and Jeremiah 12 are describing temporary prosperity, while Psalm 34:21 is describing ultimate outcome. The two are compatible because they operate on different time horizons.

The harmonization has force where the texts themselves signal the long-term framing. Psalm 73 explicitly resolves its complaint by retreating to the sanctuary and recognizing the final destruction of the wicked (Psalm 73:17-20), which fits the long-term reading. The problem is that not all the texts in question allow this resolution. Job 12:6 is a flat empirical claim with no eschatological corrective in context — Job is describing the way the world actually works, and the whole book of Job refuses to resolve the problem of suffering by appeal to an afterlife (which Israelite theology of this period did not have in any developed form). Jeremiah 12:1 is a complaint addressed to God demanding an explanation, and the answer Jeremiah gets (Jeremiah 12:5) is essentially that things are going to get worse, not that the wicked will be punished.

The critical conclusion is that the Hebrew Bible preserves competing views on this question because Israelite religion went through a long, painful process of confronting the empirical failure of strict retribution and developing alternative theological frameworks to cope with it. Some texts hold to retribution. Other texts give it up and admit the wicked prosper. Still others develop a long-term framework that defers the resolution to the end of life or to the eschaton. All three frameworks coexist in the canon. The apologetic harmonization works for some texts and fails for others, which is what we would expect from a canon that preserves genuinely different theological responses to the same problem. The honest read is theological pluralism, not a single consistent doctrine.
